idiom_name: Scala 3 opaque type over (minor units, Currency) with extension methods
implementation_notes: Scala 3's opaque type makes the money wrapper a compile-time-only abstraction: opaque type Money = (Long, Currency) erases to a tuple at runtime, extension methods supply +, -, comparison and allocation, and returning Either[CurrencyMismatch, Money] instead of Money makes a cross-currency addition something the caller must handle. scala.math.BigDecimal (standard library, MathContext with HALF_EVEN by default) carries the amount when sub-minor precision is needed, as with a Price that settles into an Amount. The classic class remains justified when the model wants subtyping or Java interop, since opaque types are invisible outside their defining scope.
pitfalls: Opaque types are transparent only inside their defining scope, so the API must be complete or callers will cast their way around it.
Mixing a BigDecimal-based Price with a Long-based Amount forces an explicit setScale(0, HALF_EVEN).toLong - which is exactly where rounding must be named.
Scala 2 cannot compile opaque types, so a cross-built library needs the value-class variant as the common denominator.

variants.name: Scala 2 AnyVal value class over minor units
variants.idiom_name: final class Money[C <: Currency](val minorUnits: Long) extends AnyVal
variants.implementation_notes: On Scala 2 the wrapper is an AnyVal value class with operator methods: the JVM erases it in local and field positions, so it costs nothing in the common case, but it boxes inside collections and generics and cannot define equals/hashCode of its own, which leaves equality structural on the underlying value. It is the same zero-cost idea as the Scala 3 opaque type with weaker guarantees, and it is the version to use while the codebase still cross-builds.
pitfalls: An AnyVal value class has exactly one val, so the currency must live in a type parameter, a companion encoding or an enclosing class.
Boxing appears in List[Money], Option[Money] and similar generic positions, where the performance argument evaporates.
Value classes cannot override equals/hashCode, so equality is the underlying value's unless a universal trait is involved.

variants.name: squants Money with an implicit MoneyContext
variants.implementation_notes: squants models Money as a Quantity whose units of measure are Currencies, adding MoneyContext with a default currency and exchange rates so cross-currency operations either find an implicit rate or raise NoSuchExchangeRateException, and it keeps BigDecimal precision where the generic Quantity API would narrow to Double. Choose it when the codebase already models units of measure; skip it when the money type must serialize to a fixed wire format without the library's own API in the way.
variants.code_sketch:
import squants.market.{Money, MoneyContext, USD}
implicit val ctx: MoneyContext = MoneyContext(USD, currencies, exchangeRates)
val price = USD(BigDecimal("12.99"))     // the BigDecimal apply, not the Double overload
val total = price * 3
pitfalls: Some apply overloads take Double, which reintroduces the precision problem; the BigDecimal overloads are the ones to use.
The implicit context makes conversion invisible at the call site, which is convenient and awkward to audit.
Dividing Money by Money yields a CurrencyExchangeRate, not an amount, because a rate is not money.
